summary: Describes how link-layer status information from various access technologies, such as link up and down events, can help IP quickly detect that a host has attached to a different network. It gives a non-exhaustive catalogue of what well-known technologies can provide. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device joins a new network, the radio layer finds out first, and the IP layer finds out last. RFC 4957 lists what each kind of network can report at that moment, so the IP layer can start reconfiguring itself straight away instead of waiting for a router advertisement.

questions: how does ip detect network attachment changes
how does device detect network change
what is a link layer event notification
subtitle: How the radio layer tells the IP layer that a device has joined a new network, so its address can be reconfigured quickly.

tldr.problem: When a device moves to a different network, IP has to find a new address, gateway and name server, and the network-layer signals that would tell it are often slow or missing.
tldr.mechanism: The link layer can send a link up event as soon as it has attached to a new point, optionally with the identity of that point or the configuration parameters it was given, and the IP layer can use that to start looking for a configuration change.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational catalogue of what GPRS, cdma2000, IEEE 802.11 and IEEE 802.3 can report. It defines no detection process of its own and adds no protection against spoofed notifications.

facts.value: None: the address received contains no valid prefix

today: RFC 4957 is an Informational document from August 2007 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a non-exhaustive catalogue of the link-layer status information available from GPRS, cdma2000, IEEE 802.11 and IEEE 802.3, and it leaves the detection process itself to the DNA solution specifications.

sections.title: Why the Link Layer Should Tell IP What Happened
sections.content:
It is not uncommon for a node to change its point of attachment to the network. This can happen because of mobile usage, such as a mobile phone moving among base stations, or nomadic usage, such as the road-warrior case.

A node that changes its point of attachment may also change its IP subnet, and therefore need to reconfigure IP-layer parameters such as its IP address, its default gateway information and its DNS server address. Detecting the subnet change can usually use network-layer indications, such as a change in the advertised prefixes for IPv6, but such indications may not always be available to the node when it changes its point of attachment.

Link-layer event notifications can help IP detect configuration changes expeditiously. The document provides a non-exhaustive catalogue of the information available from some access technologies and discusses how the IP layer should interpret it. It is not intended to specify or change the behaviour of those access technologies in any manner.

Additional information can be conveyed along with the event, such as the identifier of the network attachment point, for example the IEEE 802.11 Basic Service Set Identification and the Service Set Identifier, or network-layer configuration parameters obtained through the link-layer attachment process if they are available. Such notifications can in some circumstances be used to speed up the inter-subnet movement detection and reconfiguration process. For example, a notification that the node has established a new link-layer connection may be used to probe the network immediately for a possible configuration change. Without such a notification, IP has to wait for indications that are not immediately available, such as the receipt of the next scheduled router advertisement or the unreachability of the default gateway.

It should be noted that a link-layer event notification does not always translate into a subnet change. Even if the node has torn down a link-layer connection with one attachment point and established a new connection with another, it may still be attached to the same IP subnet. Several IEEE 802.11 access points can be attached to the same IP subnet, and moving among them does not warrant any IP-layer configuration change.
sections.plainLanguage: The radio layer knows first that a device has attached somewhere new. Without a signal from it, the IP layer has to wait for the next router advertisement or for the old gateway to stop answering, both of which take time.

sections.title: How a Link Up Event Is Delivered
sections.content:
Link-layer event notifications are one of the inputs to the process of detecting network attachment. Such a process is likely to take other inputs, such as the presence of advertised prefixes or the reachability of default gateways, before deciding whether the IP-layer configuration must be updated. While a link-layer notification by itself may not be all the input the process needs, it can at least be useful for prompting the process to collect further information. The node may send a router solicitation as soon as it learns that a new link-layer connection is established.

The event considered most useful is the link up event, which signifies a state change associated with the interface becoming capable of communicating data packets. The notification is provided to the IP layer after the event concludes successfully. The link up events and notifications are associated with a network interface, and the IP module may receive simultaneous independent notifications from each of the network interfaces on the node.

The event is managed by the link layer of the node through the execution of link-layer protocols and mechanisms, and once it completes successfully its notification is delivered to the IP layer. By the time the notification is delivered, the link layer must be ready to accept IP packets. Each time an interface changes its point of attachment, a link up event should be generated.

There is a non-deterministic usage of the link up notification, to accommodate implementations that want to indicate the link is up even though data transmission may still be blocked in the network, as in the IEEE 802.3 discussion later in the document. A link up notification may be generated with an appropriate attribute conveying its non-deterministic nature, or the link-layer implementation may choose to delay the notification until the risk conditions cease to exist. If a non-deterministic link up was generated, another link up must follow as soon as the link layer is capable of generating a deterministic notification, and the attributes may indicate whether the packets transmitted since the previous notification were presumed blocked or allowed by the network. Consumers may treat the deterministic link up that follows differently, for example the second event need not trigger a confirmation process if the first one already did.

A node may have to change its IP-layer configuration even when the link-layer connection stays the same, as in the case of IPv6 subnet renumbering, so a link-layer notification is not a mandatory indication of a subnet change. A link up notification may optionally deliver information relating to the attachment point, such as the identity of the attachment point, for example a base station identifier, or the IP-layer configuration parameters associated with the attached subnet, such as the subnet prefix and the default gateway address. Merely knowing that a new connection is established may prompt the detection process to look for further clues, while the auxiliary information may constitute further clues and sometimes the final answers. Where there is a one-to-one mapping between attachment point identifiers and IP-layer configurations, learning the former can reveal the latter.
sections.plainLanguage: The notification reaches the IP layer only once the radio link has finished its own handshake, so the IP layer can send packets straight away. It may carry extra facts, such as which network was joined or what address was handed out, and the IP layer can use those instead of asking around.

sections.title: Cellular Networks: GPRS and cdma2000
sections.content:
The GPRS architecture consists of a Radio Access Network and a packet domain Core Network. The Radio Access Network is composed of Mobile Terminals, a Base Station Subsystem and Serving GPRS Support Nodes. The IP Core Network acts as the transport backbone of user datagrams between those nodes and Gateway GPRS Support Nodes, and the gateway ensures connectivity with external networks such as the Internet or local area networks, acting as the default IP gateway for the terminal.

A terminal that wants IP connectivity first establishes a connection to the GPRS network and one or more PDP Context associations between itself and the gateway. Only after the PDP Context has been established, and after address autoconfiguration and tunnelling have taken place, can its IP packets be forwarded to and from its remote peers. The aim of establishing the context is also to provide IP-level configuration on top of the GPRS link-layer attachment. Successful establishment of a PDP Context signifies the availability of IP service, so this link-layer event generates a link up event notification sent to the IP layer.

A terminal may establish a secondary PDP Context while reusing the IP configuration from a previously established and active context. Such a secondary context provides no additional information to the IP layer and only allows another quality of service profile to be used, so its activation does not usually generate a link up event, since it does not require new IP parameters.

With IPv4, the auxiliary information carried with the notification is the IPv4 address of the terminal obtained as part of the PDP Context. With IPv6, the activation response does not come with a usable address: the address received from the gateway in the PDP address field does not contain a valid prefix, and the terminal only uses the interface identifier from that field to form a link-local address, which it then uses to obtain a valid prefix, by stateless or stateful address configuration. So no IPv6-related auxiliary information is provided to the IP layer.

For cdma2000-based 3GPP2 packet data services, the major components are the Mobile Station, the Radio Access Network made up of base station transceivers, base station controllers and the packet control function, and the Network Access Server known as the Packet Data Switching Node, which serves as the default IP gateway. These networks use the Point-to-Point Protocol as the link-layer protocol between the mobile station and the packet data switching node. Before any IP packets may be sent or received, the Point-to-Point Protocol must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and the IP Control Protocol, or its IPv6 equivalent, must reach the Opened state. When those states are reached, a link up event notification is delivered to the IP layer.

For the 3GPP2 Simple IPv4 service, the IP Control Protocol enables configuration of an IPv4 address on the mobile station, and that address is provided as the auxiliary information along with the link up notification. The IPv6 equivalent does not provide an IPv6 address, but the interface identifiers for the local and remote endpoints of the link. Since there is no standards-mandated correlation between the interface identifier and other IP-layer configuration parameters, this information is deemed not useful for detecting network attachment, though it may be provided as auxiliary information for other uses.
sections.plainLanguage: On a cellular network the notification comes when the data session is set up, because that is when the device is given its address and a working path to the internet. With IPv4 the address comes with the notification; with IPv6 it does not, so the IP layer has to find out for itself.

sections.title: IEEE 802.11 Wireless
sections.content:
IEEE 802.11-based WiFi networks are the wireless extension of local area networks. The standards available at the time were IEEE 802.11b, 802.11g and 802.11a, and they define both the MAC layer and the physical layer. The MAC layer is the same for all of them.

Two operating modes are available, infrastructure mode and ad-hoc mode. In infrastructure mode all link-layer frames are transmitted to an access point, which forwards them to the final receiver, and a station establishes an association with an access point in order to send and receive IP packets. In a WiFi network that uses Robust Secure Network, successful completion of the four-way handshake between the station and the access point commences the availability of IP service, and the link up event notification is generated upon that event. In non-RSN-based networks, a successful association or re-association event causes a link up notification to be sent to the IP layer.

As part of the link establishment the station learns the BSSID and the SSID associated with the access point. The BSSID is a unique identifier of the access point, usually set to the MAC address of its wireless interface. The SSID carries the identifier of the Extended Service Set, the set composed of access points and associated stations that share a common distribution system. Both may be provided as auxiliary information along with the link up notification.

Unfortunately this information does not give a deterministic indication of whether the IP-layer configuration must be changed on movement. There is no standards-mandated one-to-one relation between the BSSID and SSID pairs and IP subnets. An access point with a given BSSID can connect a station to any one of multiple IP subnets, an Extended Service Set with a given SSID may span multiple IP subnets, and the SSIDs are not globally unique, since the same SSID may be used by multiple independent Extended Service Sets. Nevertheless, the BSSID and SSID information may be used in a probabilistic way by the detection process, and so it is provided with the link up event notification.

In ad-hoc mode, stations in range communicate directly with each other, without any infrastructure or intermediate hop, and the set of communicating stations is called an Independent Basic Service Set. Only station services are available there: authentication, deauthentication, privacy and delivery of MAC service data units. Stations do not associate with each other, and may exchange data frames in state 2, authenticated and not associated, or even in state 1, unauthenticated and unassociated, if the Distribution System is not used. If authentication is performed, a link up indication can be generated upon authentication. For link layer identification, both the BSSID, which is a random MAC address chosen by a station of the Independent Basic Service Set, and the SSID may be used to identify a link, but not to make any assumptions about the IP network configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: On WiFi the notification comes when the device has joined an access point and, if the network is secured, completed the key handshake. The names of the access point and of the network come with it, but they do not reliably say which IP subnet the device is on, so they are only a hint.

sections.title: Ethernet and the Extra Delay of Bridging
sections.content:
IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD, commonly referred to as Ethernet, is the most commonly deployed local area network technology in use today, and it is specified by a physical layer and medium access control layer specification. To connect different LANs together into a larger network, 802.3 LANs are often bridged together. In Ethernet networks, hosts are connected by wires or by optic fibre to a switch, a bus, a repeater or directly to another Ethernet device.

IEEE 802.3 specifies its own link monitoring mechanism, defined for some but not all classes of media, to determine whether the physical medium is ready for frame transfer. This Link Integrity Test operation is used to identify when packets are able to be received on an Ethernet segment, and it applies to both wired and optical physical layers, although details vary between technologies, with link pulses in twisted pair copper and light levels in fibre. The tests typically occur at initial physical connection time, for example at the auto-negotiation stage, and periodically afterwards.

The status of the link as determined by the test is stored in a variable called link_status, which has possible values of FAIL, READY and OK. In FAIL state the tests have failed, in READY state the link segment has passed the integrity tests but auto-negotiation has not completed, and in OK state the medium is able to send and receive packets. On transition to a particular state the physical medium attachment subsystem generates an indication, and indications of OK state may be used to generate a link up event notification. These indications do not definitively ensure that packets will be able to be received through the bridge domain.

That is where bridging comes in. Ethernet networks commonly consist of LANs joined together by transparent bridges, usually implemented as switches. Transparent bridges require the active topology to be loop free, achieved through the Spanning Tree Protocol or the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol. These protocols exchange Bridge Protocol Data Units, which leads to the blocking of ports where required. By default the spanning tree protocol does not know whether a particular newly connected piece of Ethernet will cause a loop, so it blocks all traffic from and to newly connected ports, with the exception of some unbridged management frames, until it determines that the port can be connected in a loop-free manner. For these technologies, even though the link layer appears available, no data packet forwarding occurs until that determination is made.

A host connected to a bridge port does not receive any explicit indication that the bridge has started forwarding packets, so it may not know when the spanning tree operations have completed, or when it is safe to inform the upper layers to transmit packets. Where it is not known that forwarding operations are available, a host should assume that one of the spanning tree protocols is being performed, and hosts may listen to the spanning tree and 802.1AB messages to gain further information about the timing of full connectivity. It is not easy for a host to distinguish between disabled bridge ports and non-bridge ports with no active transmitters on them, since disabled ports have no traffic on them and incur 100% sender loss.

If no bridge configuration messages are received within the Bridge_Max_Age interval, which defaults to 20 seconds, it is likely that there is no visible bridge whose port is enabled for bridging, since at least two hello messages would have been lost. Upon this timeout a link up notification is generated, if one has not been already. If a bridge protocol data unit is received and the adjacent bridge is running the original Spanning Tree Protocol, the host cannot successfully send packets until at least twice the ForwardDelay value in the received message has elapsed, and a link up notification is generated after that time. If the previous notification was non-deterministic, the new one includes an attribute saying that packets sent within the prior interval were lost. If the bridge is identified as performing the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol, it instead waits Bridge_Max_Age after packet reception, as advertised in the message's Max Age field, before forwarding, and for ports known to be point-to-point through auto-negotiation this delay is abbreviated to 3 seconds after auto-negotiation completes.

The recently defined 802.1AB Link-Layer Discovery Protocol provides information to devices that are directly adjacent on the local LAN. It sends information periodically and at link status change time, and may contain a System Capabilities element describing the MAC- and IP-layer functions a device is currently using. Where a host receives it indicating that no bridging is occurring on the transmitter, no delays for spanning tree calculation are applied to packets sent through that transmitter, which would allow the generation of a link up notification. If it indicates that the transmitter is a bridge, the host's advertisement that it is a station only may tell the bridge not to run the spanning tree protocol and may immediately allow forwarding. Because the protocol is new and not widely deployed, it is unclear how it will eventually affect detection of network attachment in IPv4 or IPv6 networks.

Other heuristics are available in 802.3 networks, where network interface cards are often capable of returning a speed and duplex indication to the host, and changes in these characteristics may indicate a connection to a new layer 2 network. The summary of the section is that link-layer indications in Ethernet-like networks are complicated by additional unadvertised delays due to spanning tree calculations, which may cause the re-indication or retraction of indications previously sent to the upper layers.
sections.plainLanguage: On a wired network the cable may be ready before the switch is ready, because the switch has to check for loops before it forwards anything. The host is not told when that finishes, so it either waits a fixed time or listens to the switch's messages to work it out.

sections.title: Spoofed Notifications and the Evil Twin
sections.content:
Attackers may spoof various indications at the link layer, or manipulate the physical medium directly, in an effort to confuse the host about the state of the link layer. For instance, attackers may spoof error messages or disturb the wireless medium to cause the host to move its connection elsewhere or even to disconnect, and they may also spoof information to make the host believe it has a connection when in reality it does not. In addition, wireless networks such as 802.11 are susceptible to an attack called the Evil Twin attack, where an attacker sets up an access point with the same SSID as a legitimate one and gets the user to connect to the fake access point instead of the real one. These attacks may cause the use of non-preferred networks or even denial of service.

This specification provides no protection of its own for the indications from the lower layers, but the vulnerabilities can be mitigated through techniques in other parts of the protocol stack. It is recommended that authentication, replay protection and integrity protection of link-layer management messages are enabled when available. The IEEE 802.1ae standard, for example, defines such mechanisms for IEEE 802-compliant MAC layers. The protocol stack may also use some network-layer mechanisms to achieve partial protection: SEND, defined in RFC 3971, could be used to confirm secure reachability with a router. Network-layer mechanisms are, however, unable to deal with all problems, such as insecure lower-layer notifications that lead to the link not functioning properly.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in the notification is trustworthy on its own, because anyone nearby can send a false one, and a fake access point with the same name can attract the device. The protection has to come from elsewhere in the stack, such as authenticating the link-layer messages.

viz.caption: WHAT THE LINK LAYER TELLS THE IP LAYER

items.title: The link up event
items.text: Signifies that the interface has become capable of passing data packets, and is delivered once the link layer has completed its own protocols and is ready to accept IP packets.

items.title: Non-deterministic link ups
items.text: Some link layers know the link is up but that data may still be blocked in the network. The notification can say so, and a deterministic one follows later.

items.title: Auxiliary information
items.text: The identity of the attachment point, such as a base station identifier, or the IP configuration parameters of the attached subnet, such as the prefix and the default gateway.

items.title: Not proof of a subnet change
items.text: The IP layer can have to reconfigure even when the link stays the same, as in IPv6 subnet renumbering, so a notification is not a mandatory indication of a subnet change.
